# External Content-Guard Holdout Sources

`holdout.jsonl` is an **external holdout**. It measures how Judikt's deterministic content guard generalises to prompt-injection data written independently of its rules. It must never be used to tune rules or thresholds. It was evaluated once against the pre-change rules (`docs/evidence/content-guard-external-baseline-2026-10-24.json`) and once after the recall changes (`docs/evidence/content-guard-external-after-2026-10-24.json`); re-run it only to report, never to iterate.

The file is generated by `scripts/build_external_holdout.py` from the pinned commits below. The script verifies every source file against `sources.lock.json` before converting it.

| Source | Repository | Pinned commit | Licence | Files used |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BIPIA | https://github.com/microsoft/BIPIA | `a004b69ec0dd446e0afd461d98cb5e96e120a5d0` | MIT, Copyright (c) Microsoft Corporation | `benchmark/text_attack_test.json`, `benchmark/code_attack_test.json` (attack strings authored by the BIPIA project, MIT); `benchmark/email/test.jsonl` (EmailQA contexts derived from OpenAI Evals invoices data, MIT per BIPIA's LICENSE) |
| InjecAgent | https://github.com/uiuc-kang-lab/InjecAgent | `f19c9f2c79a41046eb13c03c51a24c567a8ffa07` | MIT, Copyright (c) 2023 Qiusi Zhan | `data/test_cases_dh_base.json`, `data/test_cases_ds_base.json` (125 cases sampled deterministically from each), `data/user_cases.jsonl` |

Source-file sha256 values are in [`sources.lock.json`](sources.lock.json).

## Licence review

- BIPIA's LICENSE grants MIT for the repository except the listed third-party datasets. The attack files are not among them. Its code contexts (Stack Exchange) and table contexts (WikiTableQuestions) are CC BY-SA 4.0, whose share-alike terms are incompatible with redistributing derived samples under this repository's Apache-2.0 licence, so they are **not used**. Its WebQA and Summarization contexts must be generated by users from sources with their own terms and are **not used**.
- InjecAgent is MIT. Its tool-response cases already embed the attacker instruction in a realistic tool output and are used as-is.
- `deepset/prompt-injections` (Hugging Face, Apache-2.0) was evaluated as a candidate but could not be downloaded in the build environment, so it is **not included**. To add it, extend the build script with a downloader and pin the dataset revision and file sha256.

## Conversion

Every record uses the corpus JSONL schema plus a `wrapper` field naming how the payload was embedded:

| Records | Label | Surface | Wrapper |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 125 BIPIA text and code attacks | attack | `tool_result` | Cycled through `readme`, `issue_body`, `web_page`, `email`, and `log`. Surrounding lines come from the benign templates of Judikt's existing corpus. |
| The same 125 BIPIA attacks | attack | `tool_description` | `tool_description` (a one-sentence tool description followed by the payload) |
| 250 InjecAgent cases | attack | `tool_result` | `injecagent_tool_response` (InjecAgent's own tool response, unchanged) |
| 50 BIPIA EmailQA contexts | benign | `tool_result` | `bipia_email_context` (unchanged) |
| 85 InjecAgent user-tool responses | benign | `tool_result` | `injecagent_template_with_judikt_benign_fill`: each of the 17 tool-response templates with its attacker-instruction slot filled by five lines from Judikt's benign corpus |

Limitations: benign coverage is smaller than attack coverage and is tool-result only. The InjecAgent benign fills reuse Judikt's own benign lines, so they measure false positives caused by the surrounding tool-output structure rather than by novel benign prose. The separate real-documentation benign measurement (`scripts/measure_real_docs_fpr.py`) is the primary false-positive check.
